messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Vignette:
Randall Kowalski is a 66-year-old married software engineer of Polish-American descent who was referred for a psychological assessment following a conversation with his primary care physician, during which he disclosed, for the first time in his adult life, that he had grown up in a household defined by violence. He arrived at the intake appointment wearing a long-sleeved shirt despite the warm weather, sat with his arms close to his sides, and spoke in the measured, careful way of someone who has spent decades choosing his words with precision.

Randall was the youngest of three children raised by a father who worked irregular hours and drank heavily. The abuse was not random — it followed a recognizable pattern. His father would return home in the early hours, and if Randall stirred or made noise, he would be pulled from bed and beaten, often with a leather belt, sometimes with open hands across the face and back. What Randall remembers most viscerally is the cold — the shock of being dragged from warm blankets into the unheated hallway, his skin contracting against the chill before the blows came. Cold air and cold surfaces became inseparable from what followed. He also remembers the way his heart would begin pounding before he could fully wake, as though his body registered the creak of the floorboards and the smell of alcohol before his mind had assembled the situation into meaning. He learned, very young, that his body knew danger faster than his thoughts could.

He carried this knowledge quietly into adulthood. He married in his thirties, built a stable career in software development, and told himself, as many survivors do, that the past was simply past. For decades this held well enough. Then, in his early sixties, a routine cardiac stress test required technicians to apply cold gel electrodes to his chest. The sudden cold against his skin — clinical, impersonal — produced a response that startled him badly. His heart rate spiked under the monitor leads, and as he felt it racing, the sensation looped back on itself: the pounding in his chest was itself a trigger, pulling a memory of lying rigid in the dark, heart hammering, waiting. He left the appointment shaken and did not return for the follow-up.

In the months that followed, Randall found himself monitoring the temperature of every room he entered. In winter, he avoided going outdoors without extensive preparation, not for comfort but because the cold air on exposed skin produced a tightening dread he could not rationalize away. At work, where he operates largely independently from a home office, he began declining the occasional in-person team meetings he had previously tolerated, telling colleagues he preferred remote collaboration. What he could not tell them was that the prospect of someone clapping him on the shoulder in greeting — something that had happened unremarkably for years — had become intolerable. He had come to believe that being touched without warning was a form of exposure to something genuinely dangerous, and when it happened, his body confirmed this belief immediately: a lurch of alarm, muscles tensing before he had formed a single thought.

His wife, Elena, noticed that he flinched when she reached for him in the kitchen, that he had stopped sitting beside her on the sofa, that he seemed to scan rooms when they entered them — his eyes moving to countertops, tools, anything that could be lifted or swung. He had not explained this to her, partly because he was certain that no explanation would be adequate, and partly because he had come to feel that he existed at a permanent remove from other people, including her. He was certain that people could not truly be trusted, that warmth and safety were provisional at best, and that vigilance was simply the honest response to a world that had always been capable of turning without warning.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment three months ago when Elena took his hand during a film they were watching at home and he pulled away sharply, then watched her face fall. He had come to believe, in some quiet, settled way, that he was permanently outside the ordinary life other people inhabited. What he most hopes, arriving at this appointment at sixty-six, is to discover whether that belief is actually true.
